children.html: Relating trait and domain mental toughness to complex task learning q
Jay H. Hardy III ⇑ , Ruth A. Imose, Eric Anthony Day
Department of Psychology, University of Oklahoma, Norman, Oklahoma, 73019, United States
Article history: Received 19 November 2013 Received in revised form 10 April 2014 Accepted 13 April 2014 Available online 7 May 2014
Keywords: Mental toughness Complex task learning Adaptive performance Predictive validity Incremental validity

Mental toughness is considered by many in the popular media and in sports psychology to be an important construct underlying success in learning and performance. However, despite a long conceptual history, little work has empirically examined the relationships between mental toughness and key learning and performance outcomes. Thus, the purpose of this laboratory study was to examine the incremental predictive validity of trait-based and domain mental toughness scores in the context of learning a complex computer task using a variety of cognitive, affective, and skill-based criteria, including a test of adaptive performance. Results revealed no relationships between trait-based mental toughness and any learning criteria. In contrast, scores from a multidimensional domain mental toughness scale explained variance in post-practice self-efficacy and performance beyond that explained by GMA, prior experience, baseline performance, pre-practice self-efficacy, goal orientation, and core self-evaluations, and was indirectly related to adaptive performance via post-practice self-efficacy and performance. Self-belief was the mental toughness subscale primarily responsible for the incremental validity. Results are discussed in terms of the implications for the conceptualization and predictive validity of mental toughness.

When witnessing successful individuals perform at peak capacity, it is natural to wonder what characteristics allowed them to succeed in their domain where others failed. One such characteristic advocated in the popular media and in sports psychology is mental toughness, generally described as the capability to cope with the pressure of difficult circumstances and to rebound from failure (Goldberg, 1998). Many in the popular press cite mental toughness as a characteristic that distinguishes great performers or when explaining why some do not live up to their potential. Proponents claim mental toughness facilitates learning, performance, and adaptability through resiliency, focus, and determination (Goldberg, 1998).

However, despite a long conceptual history in popular thinking and in psychology beginning with research on tough-mindedness (Cattell, Blewett, & Beloff, 1955), definitions of mental toughness remain nebulous. The term mental toughness is frequently used to refer to a wide range of positive characteristics that aid in coping with difficult situations. For example, Vince Lombardi described

mental toughness as ''many things and rather difficult to explain. Its qualities are sacrifice and self-denial... It's a state of mind – you could call it 'character in action''' (Lombardi, 2010). Although these characteristics are likely relevant to achievement, such definitions are markedly ambiguous. Consequently, much of the research on mental toughness to date has focused on developing and refining its operational definitions (e.g., Fourie & Potgieter, 2001; Thelwell, Weston, & Greenlees, 2005) or on debates surrounding its factor structure (e.g., Clough, Earle, Perry, & Crust, 2012; Gucciardi, Hanton, & Mallett, 2013).

Despite conceptual advancements, surprisingly little empirical research has directly examined the relationship between mental toughness and learning and performance outcomes, much less its incremental validity relative to established predictors. Moreover, although trait-based and domain conceptualizations have been proposed, little if any empirical research has compared the criterion-related validity of trait-based versus domain mental toughness. Accordingly, the purpose of the present study was to examine the predictive validity of mental toughness scores in the context of learning a complex task, specifically a complex computer game that involved strong cognitive and perceptual-motor demands. The predictive validity of a generic, trait-based measure was compared to that of a domain measure across a variety of cognitive, affective, and skill-based criteria, including a test of adaptive performance in which participants encountered unanticipated novel performance demands (Kraiger, Ford, & Salas, 1993). Additionally, we examined the extent to which mental toughness

explained variance in criterion scores beyond that explained by other predictors of learning and performance (i.e., ability, experience, self-efficacy, goal orientation, and core self-evaluations).

Much of the published work on mental toughness has been qualitative in nature involving interviews with successful individuals thought to possess high levels of mental toughness (e.g., Jones, Hanton, & Connaughton, 2007). Yet, few studies have empirically examined the outcomes of mental toughness directly. Studies that have reported the effects of mental toughness on performance generally have found small, nonsignificant relationships (e.g., Dennis, 1978) or did not account for the influence of other commonly examined predictors of performance that likely correlate with mental toughness (e.g., Crust & Clough, 2005). This is problematic considering that mental toughness shares conceptual similarities with established predictors of achievement such as core self-evaluations (Judge & Bono, 2001), self-efficacy (Stajkovic & Luthans, 1998), and goal orientation (Payne, Youngcourt, & Beaubien, 2007). Specifically, aspects of core self-evaluations (i.e., a positive self-concept) and self-efficacy (i.e., confidence in one's capabilities) overlap with self-belief, emotional control, and resiliency aspects of mental toughness. Furthermore, goal orientation (i.e., types of goals individuals implicitly pursue in achievement contexts) bears similarities with challenge, task-focused attention, commitment, and desire to succeed aspects of mental toughness. Additionally, general mental ability (GMA; Schmidt & Hunter, 2004) and domain experience (Quiñones, Ford, & Teachout, 1995) may lead to the development or expression of mental toughness, thus confounding the relationships between mental toughness and achievementrelated outcomes. Alternatively, mental toughness may facilitate the development of domain experience and skill and thus yield indirect effects on distal achievement-related outcomes through initial levels of self-efficacy and skill.

In the present study, we sought to examine if mental toughness incrementally predicted learning outcomes beyond these commonly examined predictors. Examining a construct's incremental validity is an important step in establishing its practical and theoretical utility. Furthermore, given that mental toughness is multidimensional, the predictive validities of domain mental toughness subscales were examined to develop a better understanding of what specific dimensions of mental toughness are particularly important to learning and performance.
• - Research Question 1: Does mental toughness yield incremental predictive validity above established predictors of achievement?
• - Research Question 2: Which dimension(s) contribute the most to the incremental validity of mental toughness?

At present, it remains unclear whether mental toughness is best operationalized as a stable personality trait or as a domain-specific construct. Early conceptualizations of mental toughness considered it to be a stable, trait-like variable (Cattell et al., 1955; Tutko & Richards, 1972) and many commonly used measures are trait-based (Clough, Earle, & Sewell, 2002; Middleton, Marsh, Martin, Richards, & Perry, 2004). However, others conceptualize mental toughness as a domain-specific and developable skill (e.g., Goldberg, 1998) and measure it accordingly (e.g., Gucciardi, Gordon, & Dimmock, 2009). This study addressed differences between these approaches by comparing the predictive validities of a short-form version of the trait-based Mental Toughness Questionnaire (i.e., the MT18) with a domain scale developed

specifically for the criterion task of interest. Often, the distinction between trait-based and domain-specific individual differences is not clear, as many distal traits are mediated by more proximal state-based individual differences. However, because differences across operationalizations can emerge in their relationships with performance, such comparisons are useful nonetheless. In the current study, we expected that a domain-specific measure would predict learning outcomes better based on the reasoning that domain mental toughness is more proximal and relevant to criterion scores.
- Hypothesis: Domain mental toughness will be more strongly related to learning criteria than trait mental toughness.

One-hundred twenty young-adult males (Mage = 19.33, SD = 1.77) attending a large, public university in the southwestern U.S. participated in this study for partial fulfillment of a research requirement for their introductory psychology course. Seventyfour percent of the participants self-reported as White or Caucasian, 9% as Black or African American, 7% as Asian, 6% as Latino, and 3% as Native American.

The criterion task was Unreal Tournament 2004 (UT2004; Epic Games, 2004), a commercially available first-person-shooter computer game. Using weapons, the objective of UT2004 is to destroy computer-controlled opponents (i.e., earn kills) while minimizing the destruction of one's own character (i.e., avoid deaths). Participants collect new weapons or resources to increase their character's performance capabilities. When a character is destroyed, that character reappears in a new location in the game environment with basic capabilities. Participants use a mouse and keyboard simultaneously to control their character. Additionally, participants must learn weapon strengths and weaknesses to be able to decide quickly which to use given changing circumstances. Participants receive detailed performance feedback onscreen during and at the end of every trial. Each trial lasted 3 min. Performance scores were calculated by dividing trainee's kills by the quantity of kills plus deaths plus participant rank relative to their opponents.

First, participants responded to questionnaires assessing traitbased and domain mental toughness, core self-evaluations, videogame experience, self-reported ACT score and goal orientation. Then they watched a 15-min training video explaining the basic controls, rules, and objectives of UT2004 followed by 1 min of ingame practice without opponents present. Participants then performed two trials testing baseline performance during which they were instructed to do their best, followed by a pre-practice selfefficacy questionnaire. Then, participants performed 20 practice trials, which they were instructed to view as learning opportunities, followed by four test trials; two testing post-practice performance (i.e., near/analogical transfer) and two testing adaptive performance (i.e., far/adaptive transfer) where they were again instructed to do their best. Task enjoyment and post-performance self-efficacy questionnaires were administered immediately after practice followed by the short-form of the Raven Advanced Progressive Matrices (APM). UT2004 provides objective levels of

computer-controlled opponent difficulty ranging from 1 to 8. At higher levels of difficulty, opponents are faster, more elusive, more accurate, and more varied in their tactics. For the baseline trials, practice trials, and the test of post-practice skill-based performance, participants competed against two computer-controlled opponents that were set to perform at a moderate level (5) of ingame difficulty. All of these trials were performed on the same geographical layout. For the test of adaptive performance, participants performed two trials against nine opponents set at a higher difficulty level (6) and on a larger and more varied geographical layout than before.

The 18-item short form of the MT48 (Clough et al., 2002) was used to measure trait-based mental toughness. To measure domain mental toughness, new items and subscales were developed with items framed in the context of video- and computer games. Development of this measure began with a review of the current research on mental toughness and available scales in an effort to integrate common theoretical themes and dimensions. From this search, four dimensions were identified as especially applicable to video- and computer games. Items were then developed or adapted from other scales for each of four subscales (shown in the Appendix). The four dimensions of the domain-specific mental toughness scale included self-belief, resiliency, task focus, and desire to succeed. These dimensions are conceptually consistent with the findings of qualitative research on mental toughness (e.g., Jones et al., 2007). Responses to both mental toughness scales were made on a five-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Examination of the structural validity showed the fit of a correlated four-factor model (v2 = 370.62, df = 164, CFI = .80, RMSEA = .10) was better than that of a singlefactor model (v2 = 496.71, df = 170, CFI = .69, RMSEA = .13; Dv2 (6) = 126.09, p < .01).

A composite of self-reported ACT scores and scores from the 12 item short form of the APM (Arthur & Day, 1994) were used as an index of GMA. Common self-report, Likert scales were used to measure core self-evaluations (12-items; Judge, Erez, Bono, & Thoresen, 2003), goal orientation (13-items; VandeWalle, 1997), and taskspecific self-efficacy (12-items; Hughes et al., 2013). Response options for these scales ranged from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). A four item composite was used to measure videogame experience: two asking for the frequency participants played video/computer games and first-person shooter video/computer games (1 = not at all;5= daily), and two asking for the approximate number of hours per week participants spend playing video/computer games and first-person shooter video/computer games. Baseline performance was operationalized using the mean performance of the two baseline trials.

Post-practice self-efficacy was measured using the same scale used for pre-practice self-efficacy. Task enjoyment was measured using a 6-item self-report scale (1 = strongly disagree; 5= strongly agree) developed for this study (e.g., ''I had fun learning UT2004''). Task knowledge was measured using a 20-item multiple-choice test of basic, procedural, and strategic knowledge. Post-practice skill-based performance and adaptive skill-based performance were both operationalized using the mean of their two respective trial performance scores.

Descriptive statistics, reliabilities, and correlations are provided in Table 1. Trait-based mental toughness was strongly and positively correlated with core self-evaluations (r = .67, p < .01) and learning goal orientation (r = .60, p < .01), and had a strong negative correlation with avoidance performance goal orientation (r = .58, p < .01). Correlations between trait-based mental toughness and GMA (r = .09), prove performance goal orientation (r = .07), videogame experience (r = .11), baseline performance (r = .04), and pre-practice self-efficacy (r = .17) were generally weak and not statistically significant, ps > .05. Similar to traitbased mental toughness, domain mental toughness was positively correlated with learning goal orientation, but the correlation was substantially smaller in magnitude (r = .27, p < .01). Domain mental toughness was also not significantly correlated with GMA (r = .03, p > .05). However, in contrast to trait-based mental toughness, domain mental toughness was moderately to strongly correlated with prove performance goal orientation (r = .29), videogame experience (r = .51), baseline performance (r = .34), and pre-practice self-efficacy (r = .59; ps < .01) and was not significantly correlated with core self-evaluations (r = .03) or avoidance performance goal orientation (r = .02; ps > .05).

With respect to the criteria, the results showed only small, statistically nonsignificant correlations for trait-based mental-toughness (rs = .17 to .09). In contrast, domain mental toughness showed small to moderate positive correlations with post-practice self-efficacy (r = .27), task enjoyment (r = .18), task knowledge (r = .19), and performance (r = .28; ps < .05). Although positive, the correlation between domain-specific mental toughness and adaptive performance (r = .13) was small and not statistically significant (p > .05).

Incremental validity was examined using separate hierarchical multiple regression analyses for each criterion. GMA, core selfevaluations, videogame experience, goal orientation, baseline performance, and pre-practice self-efficacy were entered in the first step as control variables. Trait-based mental toughness and the four subscales of domain mental toughness were entered in separate second steps. As shown in Table 2, the results did not support the incremental validity of trait-based mental toughness (DR2 s = .00–.02; ps > .05). Conversely, domain mental toughness provided meaningful incremental prediction of post-practice selfefficacy (DR2 = .07, p < .05) and performance (DR2 = .06, p < .05) but not of task enjoyment, task knowledge, or adaptive performance (DR2 s = .01–.02; ps > .05). The self-belief subscale contributed strongest to the prediction of learning criteria with positive regression weights for post-practice self-efficacy (b = .28, p < .05) and performance (b = .33, p < .01). With the exception of one negative regression weight for the resiliency subscale with post-practice self-efficacy (b = .24, p < .05), none of the other subscales yielded incremental validity. Collectively, these results support the Hypothesis, which predicted that domain mental toughness would be more strongly related to performance than trait-based mental toughness.

The results of the present study provided mixed support for the incremental validity of domain mental toughness but did not support the predictive validity of trait-based mental toughness. Together, these findings seem to suggest that domain-specific operationalizations of mental toughness predict achievementrelated outcomes better than trait-based operationalizations. However, our findings showed that trait-based and domain mental toughness were only weakly correlated. Moreover, the observed differences in the correlations with the other predictors suggest that trait-based and domain mental toughness may operate through distinct mechanisms. Specifically, trait-based mental toughness was related to broader, more distal predictors of achievement such as core self-evaluations and trait goal orientation that have been found to be related to distal outcomes such as job satisfaction and job performance (Judge & Bono, 2001;
Payne et al., 2007) whereas domain mental toughness was related to task performance and proximal predictors of performance and adaptability such as prior experience and self-efficacy.

Given these findings, we contend that trait-based and domain mental toughness ultimately represent distinct and independent constructs that are likely related to different criteria. Specifically, domain mental toughness speaks primarily to one's pursuit and achievement on a particular task or set of tasks in a given domain whereas trait-based mental toughness may be more broadly related to a general resiliency and determination across a variety of experiences and events. Supporting this notion, we found that domain mental toughness explained an additional 7% and 6% of the variance in post-practice self-efficacy and performance, respectively, beyond baseline performance and other predictors of learning criteria. In addition, although domain mental toughness was not directly related to adaptive performance, ancillary analyses following the recommendations of Preacher and Hayes (2004)

for testing mediation revealed that even after controlling for its relationships with the other predictors and criteria, self-belief scores yielded a small indirect effect on adaptive performance via post-practice self-efficacy and performance, standardized total indirect effect = .15; bootstrapped 95% CI [.025, .277]. In contrast, trait-based mental toughness was neither directly nor indirectly related to the learning criteria. However, the relationships between trait-based mental toughness and broader predictors of distal achievement (e.g., core self-evaluations and trait goal orientations) suggest trait-based mental toughness may be more strongly related to broader, context-independent criteria than domain mental toughness. Accordingly, future research should examine similarities and differences in the predictive validity of trait-based and domain mental toughness across a variety of proximal and distal criteria and use path analysis to identify the respective mechanisms through which mental toughness predicts various criteria. Likewise, future research on mental toughness should expand its nomological network further by examining its relationships with other general predictors of performance such as the general factor of personality (e.g., van der Linden, te Nijenhuis, & Bakker, 2010).

Although the results for domain mental toughness for predicting learning criteria were encouraging, it should be noted that despite encompassing a wide range of positive attributes, only the self-belief dimension offered incremental prediction beyond the other predictors of learning and performance. Moreover, although domain mental toughness showed indirect effects on adaptability through self-efficacy and performance, neither traitbased nor domain mental toughness directly predicted adaptive performance. Consequently, the present findings do not support the common proposition that mental toughness directly facilitates resiliency, determination, and adaptability in the presence of domain-specific difficulty and change (Goldberg, 1998), which is surprising as one might expect that mental toughness should be particularly important when adjusting to new performance challenges. To understand these effects, future work should consider the specific mechanisms through which mental toughness is thought to facilitate adaptability. For example, it has been shown that mental toughness is positively related to self-reported coping strategies such as self-talk, emotion and thought control, mental imagery, planning, focus, and effort expenditure (Crust & Azadi, 2010; Kaiseler, Polman, & Nicholls, 2009). Future research on mental toughness should directly examine the link between coping strategies resulting from mental toughness to performance adaptability.

It is important to acknowledge several limitations of the present study. First, because our sample contained only males in a laboratory setting, more research is needed to generalize the current findings to more diverse samples and real-world contexts involving consequences for failure and success. Second, we only examined the predictive validities of a single measure of trait-based mental toughness, namely the short-form of the MT48 (Clough et al., 2002). Future research should examine how other trait-based measures of mental toughness (e.g., the MTI; Middleton et al., 2004) are related to the antecedents and outcomes of achievement. Third, it is important to acknowledge that the factorial validity of the domain mental toughness measure failed to reach conventional levels of adequate fit. This limitation is consistent with the broader mental toughness literature where the structural properties of mental toughness remain a controversial topic (Clough et al., 2012; Gucciardi et al., 2013). Although progress on this issue has been made, understanding the dimensionality and structural properties of mental toughness remains an important, yet elusive goal. Finally, the correlational nature of the present study limits our ability to make causal conclusions. Future research should use experimental designs to examine how the predictive validity
of mental toughness might depend on the presence of various performance-based stressors.
